We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{2-3x}) & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{3}^{2-3x} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }({3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{-3x}) \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{3}^{-3x} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot 9\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{({3}^{-3})}^{x} \\  & =(-\frac{9}{2})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{{3}^{3}})}^{x} \\  & =(-\frac{9}{2})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{27})}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{27})}^{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13943873/assets/60c4ef99a2617fd076e6350ba68e14311ebc41b9b0f33fcc07b871198dfc103d.png)

From the graph, we see that the function increases without bound as $x$ decreases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{27})}^{x}=\infty .
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(-\frac{9}{2})\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{27})}^{x}=(-\frac{9}{2})\cdot \infty =-\infty .
$$
